title: Egress Traffic
markdown:
# Egress Traffic

A network namespace is, by design, cut off from everything — it starts with nothing but a loopback interface and no path to the outside world. Every lab so far has connected a namespace to *something specific*: the host directly (via a veth pair), or another namespace directly. This lab asks a different question: how does a namespace reach the **internet** — an address it has no direct route to, through a host that itself only has one real uplink?

This is exactly the problem Docker solves for every container it starts. A container's network namespace gets a private IP like `172.17.0.2`, yet `curl https://example.com` works inside it. Nothing on the public internet knows that address exists, let alone how to route a reply back to it. Two separate pieces of host configuration make this work, and this lab builds both of them by hand.

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/main/Linux%20Labs/Container%20Networking/egress/images/egress-overview.svg)

By the end of this lab, you will be able to:

- Explain why a Linux host does not forward packets between interfaces by default, and enable it with `sysctl`
- Explain why forwarding alone is not enough to reach the internet, and what **source NAT (masquerading)** solves
- Configure `iptables -t nat` to masquerade a namespace's outbound traffic behind the host's own address
- Verify both pieces of required state — kernel forwarding and the NAT rule — independently of each other

## The Scenario: Giving app-ns Internet Access

**app-ns** is a namespace representing an application container. It has already been wired to the host with a veth pair, the way every namespace in this module has been. The host's own external-facing interface is `eth0`, carrying the VM's real connection to the outside world (and your SSH session — read-only, as always). The goal: `app-ns` should be able to reach addresses outside its own `10.30.0.0/24` subnet, the same way a Docker container reaches `8.8.8.8` through `docker0` and the host's uplink — without the host opening a single inbound port into `app-ns`.

| What | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `app-ns` | The isolated namespace — stands in for a container |
| `veth-host` / `veth-ns` | The veth pair connecting `app-ns` to the host |
| `10.30.0.1/24` | Host-side address on `veth-host` — app-ns's gateway |
| `10.30.0.100/24` | app-ns's own address on `veth-ns` |
| `eth0` | The host's real external interface — where masqueraded traffic will appear to originate from |

> **Scope note:** this simulator checks that you configured the *correct state* — kernel forwarding turned on, and a correctly-targeted NAT rule in place — the same two things a real Linux host needs. It does not simulate actual packet-level address rewriting or real internet reachability; `ping` here, as in every lab, only checks that a route exists. Treat this lab as "wire up exactly what a real host needs for egress NAT," not as a live traffic test.

## Part 1: Reconnecting app-ns (recap)

This is the same veth pattern from earlier labs — move quickly, you've done this before.

```bash
sudo ip netns add app-ns
sudo ip link add veth-host type veth peer name veth-ns
sudo ip link set veth-ns netns app-ns
sudo ip link set veth-host up
sudo ip netns exec app-ns ip link set lo up
sudo ip netns exec app-ns ip link set veth-ns up
sudo ip addr add 10.30.0.1/24 dev veth-host
sudo ip netns exec app-ns ip addr add 10.30.0.100/24 dev veth-ns
sudo ip netns exec app-ns ip route add default via 10.30.0.1
```

At this point `app-ns` can reach `10.30.0.1` — the host — and nothing else. There is no route from `app-ns` to `eth0`'s network, and even if there were, two more things stand in the way.

## Part 2: Kernel Packet Forwarding

A machine with two network interfaces does not automatically act as a router between them. By default, the Linux kernel **drops** any packet that arrives on one interface addressed to a destination reachable only through a different interface — it only delivers packets addressed to itself. This is a deliberate security default: a workstation with a Wi-Fi card and an Ethernet port should not silently start routing traffic between the two unless an administrator explicitly asks for it.

Check the current setting:

```bash
sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward
```

```
net.ipv4.ip_forward = 0
```

`0` means forwarding is **off** — right now, even a perfectly addressed and routed packet arriving on `veth-host` destined for somewhere reachable only via `eth0` would be silently dropped by the kernel. This single flag is the difference between "a host with several interfaces" and "a router."

Turn it on:

```bash
sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1
```

```
net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1
```

Read it back to confirm:

```bash
sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward
```

**Why it matters**: this exact flag is what Docker, Kubernetes, and every VPN gateway flip on as the very first step of giving a private network outbound connectivity. Forgetting it is one of the most common reasons "I configured NAT and it still doesn't work" — the rule exists, but the kernel never even attempts to forward the packet in the first place.

## Part 3: Source NAT with MASQUERADE

Forwarding alone is still not enough. Suppose a packet from `app-ns`, source address `10.30.0.100`, does get forwarded out through `eth0` toward the internet. `10.30.0.100` is a private address — no reply can ever find its way back to it across the public internet, and most ISPs will drop a packet with a private source address at their border entirely. The packet needs its source address rewritten to something the internet can actually route a reply to: the host's own public-facing address on `eth0`.

This rewriting is **source NAT (SNAT)**. Linux offers two ways to configure it:

| Target | When to use it |
|--------|---------------|
| `SNAT --to-source <ip>` | The outgoing interface has one fixed, known IP |
| `MASQUERADE` | The outgoing interface's IP is dynamic (DHCP, a cloud instance's ephemeral address) — it automatically uses whatever address that interface currently holds |

`MASQUERADE` is the one used almost everywhere in practice — including by Docker itself for every container's default network — precisely because it doesn't need to know the interface's IP in advance. It lives in the **nat table**, in the **POSTROUTING** chain — the last point a packet passes through before actually leaving the host, which is exactly where source rewriting belongs (rewrite too early, and routing decisions further down the stack would see the wrong source).

```bash
sudo iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -o eth0 -j MASQUERADE
```

- `-t nat` — operate on the **nat** table, not the default **filter** table that `ACCEPT`/`DROP`/`REJECT` rules live in
- `-A POSTROUTING` — append to the POSTROUTING chain
- `-o eth0` — only packets leaving through `eth0` (the real external interface)
- `-j MASQUERADE` — rewrite their source address to `eth0`'s current address

List the nat table's POSTROUTING chain to confirm the rule is in place:

```bash
sudo iptables -t nat -L POSTROUTING
```

```
Chain POSTROUTING (policy ACCEPT)
target     prot opt source               destination
MASQUERADE  all  --  anywhere             anywhere
```

**Why it matters**: this is the exact mechanism behind every home router sharing one public IP across every device on the LAN, every Docker container reaching the internet through `docker0`, and every Kubernetes pod reaching out through its node. Two independent pieces of state — `ip_forward=1` and a `MASQUERADE` rule scoped to the right outgoing interface — are what turn a host with an isolated private namespace into one that namespace can use to reach anywhere.

## Part 4: Confirming the Full Picture

Two commands, read back independently, confirm everything this lab set up:

```bash
sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward
sudo iptables -t nat -L POSTROUTING
```

If the first reads `1` and the second lists a `MASQUERADE` rule targeting `eth0`, `app-ns` has everything a real Linux host needs to forward and NAT its outbound traffic — the same two steps, in the same order, that a container runtime or a NAT gateway performs automatically every time it starts.

## Conclusion

Egress connectivity for an isolated namespace is not one setting — it's two, and they solve different problems:

- **`ip_forward`** answers "will the kernel move a packet from one interface to another at all?" — off by default, because routing between interfaces is a decision, not an accident.
- **NAT (`MASQUERADE`)** answers "once forwarded, whose address does the packet leave under?" — without it, a privately-addressed packet is unroutable the moment it leaves the host.

Every container runtime, home router, and cloud NAT gateway is, underneath, running exactly these two pieces of configuration. Understanding them by hand here means the next time `docker run` "just works" on the network, you know precisely what it did for you.
